title: Earth's whole history in one day
hook: Squeeze 4.54 billion years into 24 hours. How late in the day do we turn up?

knows: Earth is very old and humans came late
doesNotKnow: how late: the last few seconds of a day
that this scale is what lets slow processes (erosion, uplift, evolution) do large things

misconception: Humans have been around for a meaningful part of Earth's history.
objective: The learner can place our species in the last few seconds of a one-day clock of Earth's history (one clock second is about 52,500 years), and can say that the clock shows how long things took, not how fast they happened.

claims.text: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old (hook and question; the clock uses 4.54 billion).
claims.source: Dalrymple, G. B. (2001), 'The age of the Earth in the twentieth century: a problem (mostly) solved', Geological Society, London, Special Publications 190, 205-221: 4.54 ± 0.05 Ga. Not opened by the builder.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-839, 2026-10-14): hook and question now say 4.54 billion, matching the readout (learner r10); previously unverified. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Re-check after the W-839 hook/question change (both now say 4.54 billion, as the readout does). Opened on PMC: Front Astron Space Sci 2023, 'Setting the geological scene for the origin of life and continuing open questions about its emergence' (PMC7615569): 'the consolidation of the Earth (4.54, Dalrymple, 2001, or ~4.53 Ga according to Kleine et al., 2009; Connelly et al., 2012)'. 'About 4.54 billion years' matches the cited Dalrymple value. Dalrymple 2001 itself is not opened; the basis is this secondary source.

claims.text: Homo sapiens appeared about 300,000 years ago, which on the clock is 23:59:54, about six seconds before midnight.
claims.source: Hublin, J.-J. et al. (2017), 'New fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco and the pan-African origin of Homo sapiens', Nature 546, 289-292 (about 315,000 years; the paper calls them early Homo sapiens). Clock arithmetic: 300,000 / 4.54e9 × 86,400 s = 5.7 s before midnight (company/domains/briefs/checks/big-ideas-cycle1-check.mjs; Demo.tsx at()). Not opened by the builder. v2 (W-635): the reveal's one dated event and its one held citation (class H).
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD (the reveal's one class-H citation, allowed by big-ideas-strategy D4). Hublin et al. 2017 (Nature) could not be opened (web blocked). The openable OpenStax Biology 2e 'The Evolution of Primates' (m66594) does not give 300,000 years (it gives archaic H. sapiens from about 500,000 years and an mtDNA ancestor about 160,000 years ago), so it cannot stand in. Clock arithmetic re-run: 300,000 / 4.54e9 x 86,400 = 5.71 s, 23:59:54, 'about six seconds' (that part is fine). Needs W-583. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Opened on PMC: Neubauer, Hublin and Gunz (2018), 'The evolution of modern human brain shape', Sci Adv 4(1): eaao5961 (PMC5783678): 'Hominin fossils from Jebel Irhoud (Morocco) that are associated with Middle Stone Age artifacts dated to around 300,000 years ago ... are either interpreted as the currently earliest known members of the H. sapiens lineage' and 'Our data show that, 300,000 years ago, brain size in early H. sapiens already fell within the range of present-day humans'. Clock re-run: 300,000 / 4.54e9 x 86,400 = 5.71 s before midnight = 23:59:54, 'about six seconds'. Hublin et al. 2017 (Nature) itself is not opened; this is a later paper by the same group. Builder (non-blocking): add the Sci Adv 2018 citation to the source field.

claims.text: The non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago (23:39 on the clock).
claims.source: Renne, P. R. et al. (2013), 'Time scales of critical events around the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary', Science 339(6120), 684-687 (66.04 Ma); impact as cause: Schulte, P. et al. (2010), 'The Chicxulub asteroid impact and mass extinction at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary', Science 327(5970), 1214-1218 (the impact's role is the consensus view; volcanism is still discussed as a contributor). Clock: 66e6/4.54e9 × 86,400 = 1,256 s before midnight = 23:39:03.96, shown as 23:39:03 (the stage floors seconds). Not opened by the builder. v2 (W-635): the asteroid and 'sudden' left the learner path (the reveal's limit no longer uses this event), so the sentence the learner sees is the stage label 'Non-bird dinosaurs end' at 23:39:03 and the date in the years-ago readout. The impact sources stay here for the record only.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Opened the ICS International Chronostratigraphic Chart 2024/12 as transcribed in PyPI pyrolite 0.3.8.post1 (data/timescale/geotimescale_202412.csv): Cretaceous ends and Cenozoic/Paleogene begin at 66 Ma. That the dinosaurs died out at the end of the Cretaceous: OpenStax Astronomy 2e 'Cosmic Influences on the Evolution of Earth' (m59829) and Concepts of Biology 'Preserving Biodiversity' (m45573), which give the older 65 Ma figure. Clock: 66e6 / 4.54e9 x 86,400 = 1,256.04 s before midnight = 23:39:03.96, shown 23:39:03 (floored). Renne 2013 and Schulte 2010 were not opened; the impact is no longer on the learner path.

claims.text: Writing dates to about 5,200 years ago (about 3200 BCE), about a tenth of a second before midnight on the clock.
claims.source: Cuneiform in Mesopotamia around 3200 BCE (source for the fact-checker: e.g. a museum or encyclopedia entry on the origins of writing; Egyptian hieroglyphs are of similar age). Clock: 5,200/4.54e9 × 86,400 = 0.099 s. Not opened by the builder. v2 (W-635): withdrawn. Writing is no longer on the stage or in the reveal (held claims cut back to the board item; the old recall used it).

claims.text: The earliest signs of life are about 3.7 billion years old (04:26 on the clock); this date is debated.
claims.source: Drafter's figure (brief #2 claim 5: 'about 3.5-3.7 billion years old, which is debated (to confirm the source)'). Candidate sources for the fact-checker: Nutman, A. P. et al. (2016), Nature 537, 535-538 (3.7 Ga stromatolite-like structures, disputed by Allwood et al. 2018, Nature 563); Schopf et al. 2018, PNAS 115(1) for 3.5 Ga microfossils. Labelled '(debated)' on the stage. Not opened by the builder. Cut if not checkable (v2, W-635); fallback: remove the 'Earliest life (debated)' event from the dial and the found list (one line in Demo.tsx EVENTS); the lesson teaches without it.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD; the brief marks it 'cut if not checkable'. Nutman et al. 2016 and Allwood et al. 2018 could not be opened. The openable OpenStax texts disagree with each other and none says 3.7: Concepts of Biology (m45512, m45513) gives stromatolite fossils from about 3.5 billion years ago, (m45511) prokaryotes 'perhaps ... approximately 3.9 billion years ago', Biology for AP Courses (m62763) 3.8. So 'debated' holds, but the 3.7 figure is not checkable, and the stage readout shows it as '3.70 billion years ago' (two decimals), more precise than a debated date allows. Fix (builder, cm-big-ideas-science's call): either apply the brief's fallback (remove the 'Earliest life (debated)' event), or re-date it to about 3.5 billion years (stromatolite fossils, OpenStax Concepts of Biology 'Prokaryotic Diversity'), which I could then verify. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Opened on PMC: Phil Trans R Soc B 2025, 'What the earliest evidence for life tells us about the early evolution of the biosphere' (PMC12329462): 'There are tenuous signs of life in rocks 3.8-3.7 billion years old ..., and abundant signs of life in younger (as of 3.5 Ga) ... rocks'; on the 3.7-3.8 Gyr Isua stromatolites, 'problems related to the highly strained and metamorphosic nature of the rocks complicate interpretations'. Front Astron Space Sci 2023 (PMC7615569): 'the oldest traces of life (an eternally controversial concept ...)'. So 'about 3.7 billion years, debated' holds, and the stage labels the event 'Earliest life (debated)'. Clock: (1 - 3.7/4.54) x 24 h = 4.44 h = 04:26. Non-blocking (cm-big-ideas-science): the readout prints '3.70 billion years ago' (toFixed(2)), which is more precise than a debated date; 'about 3.7 billion years ago' would match the sources better.

claims.text: From (James) Hutton in the 1780s, geologists argued that slow processes, given this much time, do big things (reveal: 'From Hutton in the 1780s, geologists argued that slow processes, given this much time, do big things').
claims.source: Hutton, J. (1788), 'Theory of the Earth', Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1, 209-304 (public domain; read to the society in 1785); Lyell, C. (1830-33), Principles of Geology. Builder's change from the brief draft: the brief said these geologists realised slow processes 'move continents'; continental drift came later (Wegener, 1912; plate tectonics 1960s), so the sentence says valleys and mountains. Flag for cm-big-ideas-science. Not opened by the builder. v2 (W-635): class P (public domain, 1788). Cut if not checkable; fallback: 'Given this much time, even a process too slow to see can do large things.' (no name; support: derivation from c7, the clock's scale).
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-839, 2026-10-14): reveal sentence changed to point at the Grand Canyon event on the stage (learner r10); previously unverified. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): UNVERIFIED. HELD. Learner text (Demo.tsx line 99): 'From Hutton in the 1780s, geologists argued that slow processes, given this much time, do big things: a river cutting about 0.3 mm a year carved the Grand Canyon's 1.8 km in the last two minutes.' Hutton 1788 (Trans R Soc Edinb) has no copy on an allow-listed host. The only opened source that names Hutton is a Nat Commun 2026 editorial, 'How understanding planet Earth became science' (PMC13161362). It supports the idea ('shaped by slow, continuous processes ... Uniformitarianism') but dates Hutton's proposal to 'the 1830s', which conflicts with the lesson's 1780s. I cannot settle the decade from memory, so the date stays unverified. Fix: open Hutton 1788 or a reliable history; or use the brief's fallback with no name ('Given this much time, even a process too slow to see can do large things'), support derivation. The Grand Canyon half of the sentence is c9.

claims.text: On this clock 1 hour is about 189 million years, 1 minute about 3 million years and 1 second about 52,500 years.
claims.source: 4.54e9 / 24 = 189.2 million; / 1,440 = 3.15 million; / 86,400 = 52,546. Node, 2026-10-14. v2: the reveal quotes '1 second is about 52,500 years', the same figure as the stage caption in the last-minute view.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Node: 4.54e9 / 24 = 189.17 million (stage '1 hour ≈ 189 million years'); / 1,440 = 3.153 million ('1 minute ≈ 3 million years'); / 86,400 = 52,546 ('1 second ≈ 52,500 years'; the reveal says 'about 52,500'). The recall's 3.15 million mm = 3.15 km also re-checked.

claims.text: Where it stops: the clock shows how long things took, not how fast they happened; an even spread of time can hide sudden events.
claims.source: A linear clock maps duration only; it says nothing about rates within an interval (derivation). v2 (W-635): the example (the end-Cretaceous impact, c3) left the reveal so the limit rests on no held citation.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation: the clock maps years ago to seconds linearly (Demo.tsx at()), so it encodes only when and how long; within any interval it carries no information about the rate of change, so a sudden event and a slow one over the same span look alike. Rests on no held citation.

claims.text: The Colorado River carved most of the Grand Canyon, about 1.8 km deep, in roughly the last 6 million years, about 0.3 mm a year on average; on the clock that is 23:58:05, the last two minutes (stage list: '23:58:05 Grand Canyon carved, 1.8 km'; reveal: 'A river cutting about 0.3 mm a year carved the Grand Canyon's 1.8 km in the last two minutes').
claims.source: US National Park Service, Grand Canyon geology pages (canyon about 6,000 ft / 1.8 km deep; carved by the Colorado River over about the last 5-6 million years); Karlstrom et al. (2008), 'Model for tectonically driven incision of the younger than 6 Ma Grand Canyon', Geology 36(11): 835-838. Not opened by the builder; the age of the canyon is debated (some segments are argued to be far older), which the fact-checker should weigh. Arithmetic (builder node, 2026-10-14): 1.8 km / 6 million years = 0.3 mm a year; clock second 86,400 - 6e6/4.54e9 x 86,400 = 86,285.8 = 23:58:05, 114 s before midnight.
claims.note: Added by demo-builder (W-839, 2026-10-14); needs the fact-checker. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): UNVERIFIED. HELD, narrowed. Opened on PMC: Nat Commun 2026 17: 8812, 'Tectonically driven integration of the 4.8 Ma Colorado River USA' (PMC13498593): the proto-Colorado River was integrated 'between ~8 and 4.8 Ma', with an 'initial 6–5 Ma integration pathway', and 'the Marble Canyon segment of Grand Canyon ... was incised after 5 Ma'. It also discusses the competing 'paleocanyon solution'. Nat Commun 2022 13: 4437 (PMC9343645) cites Karlstrom et al. 2014, 'Formation of the Grand Canyon 5 to 6 million years ago through integration of older palaeocanyons', and describes older paleo-drainages later captured near 6 Ma. PNAS 2025 (PMC12130896) calls the Grand Canyon's age 'controversial'. So the timing 'in roughly the last 6 million years' is supported for the river's path through the canyon. 'Most' of the canyon is not quantified in what I opened (the 2014 title says older palaeocanyons were integrated), and the age is debated, as the claim's source field says. Not supported by any opened source: the depth '1.8 km', on which the reveal's '0.3 mm a year' rests (the NPS geology pages are not allow-listed). Fix: open an NPS or USGS page for the depth, or the builder words the reveal without the depth and rate (e.g. 'the Colorado River carved most of the Grand Canyon in the last two minutes on this clock, about 6 million years').

recall.question: A river cuts 1 mm deeper each year. On the one-day clock of Earth's history, how deep does it cut in the last minute?
recall.why: One clock minute is about 3.15 million years (4.54 billion ÷ 1,440). At 1 mm a year that is about 3.15 million mm, about 3 km: slow processes do large things given deep time.
